item.title: Mediating a conflict between colleagues
item.context_text: You lead a product team of eight at a software company. Two senior members, Bekzod, the lead developer, and Claire, the product designer, have clashed repeatedly over a checkout redesign, and the tension is now affecting the whole team. You've spoken to each of them privately and arranged a joint conversation.
item.objective_text: Read the dynamics behind the conflict, run a fair joint conversation that moves towards a solution, and record what was agreed.
item.target_grammar: reframing and inclusive language (What I'm hearing from both of you is…; How might we…?)
item.cultural_note: In mediation, naming the shared goal and acknowledging both people's pressures before discussing solutions lowers defensiveness. Taking sides, even implicitly, usually entrenches the conflict.
success_conditions: Identify each person's stated position and underlying grievance
Understand what is really at stake for each of them
Open the joint conversation neutrally, with ground rules, a shared goal and a proposal
Record the agreement and the process change accurately and diplomatically

children.title: Read the team chat
children.instructions: Read this exchange from the team channel yesterday. Then answer the questions.
children.prompt_text:
Claire: Users loved the checkout redesign in testing. Can we please ship it this sprint?
Bekzod: As I've said three times now, it breaks the payment flow on older phones. Shipping it now would be reckless.
Claire: It's been "three weeks away" for two months. At some point this starts to look like obstruction.
Bekzod: If you'd involved engineering before the user tests, we wouldn't be here.
Aziz: Could we maybe take this offline?

options: The design hasn't been tested with users
It breaks the payment flow on older phones
It is too expensive to build
questions.explanation: "It breaks the payment flow on older phones."

questions.prompt: What does Claire imply by "starts to look like obstruction"?
options: Bekzod may be delaying the work deliberately
questions.explanation: She suggests the repeated delays may be intentional rather than technical.

options: Engineering wasn't involved before the user testing
questions.explanation: "If you'd involved engineering before the user tests, we wouldn't be here."

children.title: Listen to the private conversations
children.instructions: Listen to extracts from your private conversations with Claire and Bekzod. Then answer the questions.
children.prompt_text:
Claire: Honestly, I'm exhausted. I've got users asking for this, and every week there's a new reason not to ship. I don't think he respects design as a discipline.
Bekzod: She thinks I'm being difficult. I'm not. About fifteen per cent of our paying customers are on those older phones. If payments fail for them, it's my team who gets called at two in the morning, not hers.

options: She feels design is not respected
She thinks the users are wrong
questions.explanation: "I don't think he respects design as a discipline."

questions.prompt: What is at stake for Bekzod's team?
options: Being called out at night if payments fail
questions.explanation: "It's my team who gets called at two in the morning, not hers."

children.title: Open the joint conversation
children.instructions: Open the joint conversation. Set ground rules, reframe the dispute around a shared goal, acknowledge both perspectives without taking sides, and put forward a possible way forward.
children.prompt_text: Claire and Bekzod sit down, both visibly tense. They look at you.
children.goal: Lower the temperature and steer both colleagues towards a joint solution.
children.model_answer: Thank you both for coming. A couple of ground rules: one person speaks at a time, and we listen to understand rather than to reply. As I see it, you both want the same thing, a checkout that customers love and that actually works for all of them. Claire, I hear the frustration of having a validated design stuck for months. Bekzod, I hear the pressure of being the one who's called at two in the morning. So what if we looked at a phased rollout: newer devices first, and older phones once the payment issue is fixed?

children.title: Record the agreement
children.instructions: Email both of them to record what was agreed: a phased release (newer devices in the next sprint, older phones once the payment fix is tested), a review date, and earlier engineering involvement in future design work. Keep the tone appreciative and neutral.
children.prompt_text:
To: Claire, Bekzod
Subject: Today's conversation
children.goal: Record the agreement precisely and in a way that both parties will accept as fair.
children.model_answer:
Dear Claire and Bekzod,
Thank you both for such a candid and constructive conversation today. To confirm what we agreed: the redesigned checkout will be released in phases. It will go live for newer devices in the next sprint, and older phones will follow once Bekzod's team has fixed and tested the payment issue, which we expect to take no more than two sprints. For future projects, engineering will be involved from the start of the design process, before any user testing, so that technical risks surface early. I suggest the three of us review progress together in two weeks.
Best regards,
Nodira
